title: Semi-supervised retinal vessel segmentation via SAM-based teacher-student distillation with topology-aware loss.
abstract: Objective . Accurate retinal vessel segmentation is critical for early diagnosis and monitoring of ocular and systemic diseases. However, deep learning methods are often limited by scarce pixel-level annotations and the inability of standard loss functions to preserve vascular topology, leading to fragmented vessel predictions. Approach . We propose SAM-KD a semi-supervised framework that adapts the Segment Anything Model (SAM) for retinal vessel segmentation through a two-stage teacher-student distillation strategy. A LoRA-adapted SAM ViT-B teacher and a lightweight TinyViT-5 M student are first trained on limited labeled data. The frozen teacher then generates soft pseudo-labels for unlabeled images, guiding the student through feature-level and logit-level distillation. To improve structural continuity, we introduce a graph-based connectivity loss () that penalizes topological discrepancies based on Betti numbers and skeleton length. Main results . Experiments on three public benchmarks (STARE, CHASEDB1, and HRF) using only 20% labeled data show that SAM-KD outperforms other baselines across both pixel-level metrics (Dice, sensitivity, MCC) and topological metrics (clDice,,). On HRF, the proposed connectivity loss reducesby 46% compared with the strongest semi-supervised baseline (38.2 vs 71.5). The distilled TinyViT-5 M student (5.4 M parameters) achieves inference in 12 ms per image with 4.9 GB VRAM, providing aspeedup andlower memory usage than the teacher, with only a 1.1-point Dice reduction. Conclusion: SAM-KD provides an effective and annotation-efficient solution for retinal vessel segmentation by combining foundation model adaptation, hierarchical distillation, and topology-aware supervision. Its lightweight design makes it suitable for real-time clinical deployment in resource-constrained environments.

title: Multivariate searchlight decoding of structural disconnection and network features for predicting post-stroke deficits.
abstract: Objective. Lesion-symptom mapping and structural disconnection analyses have advanced our understanding of post-stroke deficits but remain predominantly based on forward inference, limiting identification of regions specifically predictive of behavioral impairment. We developed a multivariate voxelwise searchlight decoding framework for inverse inference integrating probabilistic structural disconnection with network-topological features. Approach. The analysis included 326 stroke patients from the GRECogVASC cohort assessed six months after stroke. For each patient, an age-specific probabilistic structural disconnection map was reconstructed using normative diffusion MRI tractography from 403 healthy controls. Within each voxel-centered searchlight, four features were extracted: disconnection probability, degree, clustering coefficient, and closeness centrality. Support vector machine classifiers were trained within deficit-specific decoding spaces using balanced bootstrap aggregation and majority voting to predict motor, executive, and processing-action-speed impairments. Statistical significance was assessed using 1000 permutations, retaining voxels that consistently performed above chance across bootstrap iterations. Decoding-derived regions were subsequently assessed for within-cohort individual-level classification. Main results. Initial validation focused on left and right motor impairments, identifying predictive regions primarily within the contralateral precentral gyrus, internal capsule, and corticospinal tract, with mean accuracy ranges of 68.7%-77.9%, 66.4%-74.6%, and 64.8%-71.8%, respectively. At the individual level, decoding-derived masks preserved overall classification performance, with accuracy improvements of up to 2.6% for individual deficits while reducing voxel dimensionality by up to 95.4%. Executive dysfunction and processing-action-speed deficits showed statistically above-chance but lower accuracies (54.5%-66.9%). Executive dysfunction involved predominantly left-lateralized frontotemporal regions, whereas processing-action-speed deficits involved distributed fronto-insular, temporal, parietal, visual-association, and commissural pathways. Significance. The multivariate searchlight decoding framework integrating structural disconnection and network topology provides an inverse-inference approach complementary to lesion- and disconnection-symptom mapping for identifying spatially specific predictive patterns after stroke. The strong motor findings provide proof-of-concept support for the approach, whereas the cognitive results support its extension to distributed behavioral domains while underscoring the need for independent replication before neuroanatomical or clinical interpretation (Clinical trial registration: NCT01339195).

title: Lightweight longitudinal pelvic tumor segmentation with temporal evolution awareness for adaptive radiotherapy.
abstract: Adaptive radiotherapy (ART) requires accurate longitudinal tumor segmentation to address pelvic anatomical deformation and tumor regression throughout treatment. Conventional single-timepoint models ignore temporal correlations, while existing longitudinal methods often use input-level fusion or explicit deformable registration. We propose a lightweight longitudinal segmentation framework that employs a weight-shared Siamese 3D encoder for consistent cross-timepoint feature representation and a temporal difference attention mechanism to amplify evolving tumor regions while suppressing static anatomical interference. Experiments on two longitudinal T2-weighted MRI datasets of cervical and rectal cancer showed that the proposed method outperformed the evaluated segmentation baselines. Compared with Longitudinal nnU-Net, it achieved up to 5.67 percentage-point improvements in Dice, 7.13 percentage-point improvements in IoU, and a 21.8% reduction in HD95, while introducing negligible additional parameters and maintaining fast inference. These retrospective segmentation results demonstrate the efficiency of the framework on the evaluated T2-weighted MRI datasets and support further prospective evaluation for potential integration into time-sensitive ART workflows.

title: FASA-Net: a frequency-domain-enhanced and anatomically constrained vision-language framework for automated chest x-ray report generation.
abstract: Automated radiology report generation can reduce radiologists' workloads by producing preliminary reports from medical images. However, generating chest x-ray reports remains challenging. Subtle lesions and organ boundaries may be underrepresented, visual regions may be poorly aligned with medical terminology, and long reports require coherent clinical descriptions. To address these challenges, we propose FASA-Net, a vision-language framework that combines frequency-domain enhancement with anatomical semantic constraints. Its frequency-domain pyramid attention network (FPAN) integrates frequency-domain analysis and a multiscale feature pyramid to enhance local structures and high-frequency visual details. The anatomical semantic constraint attention (ASCA) module guides cross-modal interactions between visual regions and anatomy-related terms to reduce the risk of regional misalignment and semantic hallucination. The context aggregation module (CAM) incorporates a summary of the text generated so far into decoding to improve coherence and terminological consistency. Experiments on the public IU x-ray and MIMIC-CXR datasets show competitive performance on natural language generation metrics, including BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE-L, together with improved clinical label consistency measured using CheXbert-based clinical efficacy metrics. Ablation studies, visualizations, and case studies further illustrate the contributions of FPAN, ASCA, and CAM to visual detail enhancement, anatomical semantic alignment, and contextual aggregation. FASA-Net therefore has potential as an auxiliary tool for chest x-ray report generation, although clinical deployment requires further validation using multicenter data, radiologist assessments, and prospective studies.

title: DuF-DiT: Dual-Domain Fusion Diffusion Transformer with Latent Conditional Modeling for CT Metal Artifact Reduction.
abstract: Background and objective Metal implants introduce nonlinear corruptions into computed tomography (CT) projection measurements, producing severe artifacts in reconstructed images. Dual-domain metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods combine sinogram and image information to correct corrupted projections and suppress image-domain artifacts. However, their cross-domain communication commonly relies on predefined projection operations or fixed interaction pathways. In diffusion-based MAR, sustained interaction between evolving image and sinogram representations throughout the denoising process remains insufficiently explored. Methods: We introduce the Dual-Domain Fusion Diffusion Transformer (DuF-DiT), which iteratively fuses parallel image and sinogram latent representations during denoising. Its Dual-Domain Fusion Transformer blocks combine intra-domain self-attention with bidirectional cross-attention. A difference-guided gating mechanism adaptively blends conditions from metal-affected observations and linear-interpolation (LI) priors. Denoising in a CT-adaptive latent space further reduces the computational cost of the two parallel streams. Results: On synthesized DeepLesion data, DuF-DiT achieved the highest mean structural similarity index (SSIM), competitive peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and root mean square error (RMSE), and the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) in Hounsfield units (HU), with a small mean HU bias. It also achieved the lowest Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) among the compared methods. On clinical CT data, qualitative comparisons showed reduced visible artifacts with preserved anatomical structures, while DuF-DiT yielded the numerically highest mean bone-segmentation Dice coefficient on CLINIC-metal. Ablation studies supported the complementary contributions of adaptive conditioning and bidirectional cross-domain interaction. Conclusions: The results support sustained dual-domain interaction in latent space as an effective strategy for CT metal artifact reduction, with favorable image fidelity, CT-value accuracy, and downstream bone-segmentation performance under the evaluated conditions.

title: Learning Diverse Representations via Information-Bottleneck-Optimized Mixture-of-Experts in Pulmonary Nodule Detection.
abstract: Automatically detecting pulmonary nodules via thoracic computed tomography is an effective method for screening early-stage lung cancer. Current methods treat all nodules as a single category, overlooking diverse characteristics of nodules. Moreover, existing datasets provide incomplete or no fine-grained annotations, further impeding the learning of diverse representations across nodule subsets. Our analysis reveals this oversight leads to significantly discrepant missed detection rates among subsets and yields suboptimal detection performance. To address these limitations, we propose a method called latent subset clustering of mixture of experts. Leveraging an information-bottleneck-optimized mixture of experts mechanism to cluster nodules into latent subsets and calibrate the clustering process, it learns diverse representations from these latent subsets without relying on fine-grained labels. Specifically, a backbone network first encodes inputs into embedding vectors. The routing network then clusters these embeddings into latent subsets and encourages different expert networks to learn subset-specialized representations. Subset-specialized experts tend to output strong responses for embeddings matching their assigned subsets. Finally, an expert-guided information bottleneck compression is used to calibrate the latent-subset distribution by aligning the router outputs with expert responses. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Crucially, empirical results suggest that our method learns more discriminative representations from self-discovered latent subsets than from annotated density labels. We hope it can provide novel insights into uncovering significant features via latent subsets. The code is available at https://github.com/EasyDreaming/lscmoe.

title: Brain MRI Super-Resolution with 2.5D Inter-Slice Context and Contourlet-Domain Conditioning.
abstract: High-resolution brain MRI acquisition is constrained by scan duration, signal-to-noise ratio, and motion sensitivity. This study developed a 2.5D super-resolution (SR) framework combining five-slice low-resolution (LR) context with contourlet-domain conditioning. A separate branch encodes the central LR slice using the nonsubsampled contourlet transform. Adaptive gates regulate its influence on spatial reconstruction. All inference inputs are LR-derived. The primary ×4 evaluation comprised 6,799 slices from 58 held-out IXI T1 subjects. The framework achieved 26.773 dB PSNR, 0.8945 SSIM, and 0.1184 LPIPS. PSNR exceeded HAT-S by 0.858 dB, with positive subject-level differences in all 58 subjects. The largest staged gain accompanied the introduction of three-slice context. Subject-level through-plane gradient error was 13.71% lower than in the 2D configuration. Budget-matched ×4 comparisons showed no PSNR advantage over the spatial control, while SSIM and LPIPS slightly favored the complete model. Under budget-matched ×2 training, contourlet conditioning increased PSNR by 0.013 dB. Processing prepared LR files to CPU SR outputs required 119.32 ms per slice, including NSCT preprocessing. External evaluation on 30 glioma subjects showed no consistent reconstruction or segmentation benefit from contourlet conditioning under matched training. These findings concern simulated LR degradation. Diagnostic benefit, lesion preservation, and robustness to actual acquisition conditions remain unestablished.

title: Stable training and confidence‑calibrated generation of urinary stone CT images via physics‑constrained GANs under small‑sample conditions.
abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence has become integral to modern medicine. Deep learning algorithms are widely used to assist clinical diagnosis, and medical image synthesis has become increasingly mature. However, in small-sample scenarios, synthetic images often overlook infrequent but clinically valuable lesion features. To address the challenges of training instability, insufficient authenticity, and limited clinical usability, we propose a two-stage framework based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). In the first stage, we establish a stable training and physical prior constraint framework for small-sample CT images. Specifically, we incorporate an established asymmetric normalization strategy into the WGAN-GP framework to balance generator convergence and the discriminator's Lipschitz constraint, and we embed a physical noise simulation layer at the discriminator's front end, combined with partial volume effect gradient regularization, to enhance the realism of synthesized images. In the second stage, we employ MC Dropout and deep ensemble methods to quantify uncertainty, generating uncertainty heatmaps and physically consistent confidence maps based on the Poisson-Gaussian noise model. This assists physicians in locating abnormal areas and reducing misdiagnosis risks. Through joint optimization of the generation framework, uncertainty quantification, and confidence image output, the proposed framework effectively resolves issues of mode collapse, low confidence, and poor clinical usability under small-sample conditions. The proposed framework achieves a competitive FID of 128.0, an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.072, and a high-risk recall rate of 88% for stone boundary regions, demonstrating its potential for clinically reliable synthetic CT generation.

title: Mitigating over-smoothing in Mamba via high-frequency-guided feature optimization for medical image segmentation.
abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in medical image segmentation owing to their efficient global context modeling capabilities. However, the sequential scanning mechanism of SSMs tends to induce feature over-smoothing, attenuating high-frequency lesion details and blurring irregular boundaries. In this paper, we propose HFG-Mamba, a Vision Mamba network architecture driven by high-frequency-guided feature optimization. With marginal computational and parameter overhead, the proposed architecture achieves a synergy between high-frequency prior extraction and boundary-semantic interaction. Specifically, a high-frequency prior guidance branch built upon the Discrete Wavelet Transform provides the backbone with high-frequency spatial priors. The spatial recalibration fusion block leverages these priors to counteract over-smoothing by recalibrating backbone features. The decoder further incorporates a boundary-semantic interaction module to restore boundary details degraded during upsampling. Moreover, a structure-preserving deep supervision strategy is introduced to address the optimization difficulties arising from gradient vanishing and boundary sparsity. Experiments on the ISIC17, ISIC18, and Kvasir-SEG datasets indicate that HFG-Mamba exhibits competitive performance, effectively delineating irregular boundaries and suppressing background artifacts.

title: CMRCUNet: a cross-modal calibration U-Net for acute ischaemic stroke lesion segmentation from multi-sequence MRI.
abstract: Purpose: Acute ischaemic stroke is a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, and rapid delineation of infarct lesions on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is important for supporting time-sensitive treatment decisions. Multi-sequence MRI, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), provides complementary information for characterising acute ischaemic lesions. However, many deep learning approaches process these modalities using shared encoders and direct skip connections, which may limit modality-specific feature learning and remain challenged by the severe foreground-background imbalance characteristic of stroke lesion segmentation. Method: We propose CMRCUNet, a multimodal segmentation framework that combines modality-specific residual encoders, a cross modal calibration (CMC) module, and an attention-gated decoder. The modality-specific encoders independently learn sequence-dependent representations from DWI, ADC, and FLAIR, while the CMC module performs adaptive, input-dependent weighting of modality-specific features at multiple resolution levels before decoder fusion. Focal Tversky Loss is used to address severe lesion-background imbalance. The framework is evaluated in both 2D and 2.5D configurations; the 2.5D configuration incorporates neighbouring axial slices to provide limited through-plane contextual information while retaining two-dimensional convolutional operations. Test-time augmentation (TTA) is additionally evaluated to improve inference robustness. Results: CMRCUNet was evaluated on the Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation 2022 dataset using a patient-level evaluation protocol with an independent 37-patient test cohort. The 2.5D configuration combined with TTA achieved a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.792 ± 0.142, sensitivity of 0.854 ± 0.132, specificity of 0.996 ± 0.012, and a 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 8.21 ± 8.70 mm. Conclusion: CMRCUNet provides a multimodal framework that integrates modality-specific feature extraction, adaptive CMC, attention-gated decoding, and limited inter-slice contextual information for acute ischaemic stroke lesion segmentation. The results support further investigation of adaptive CMC, particularly through external multi-centre validation.

title: Development and validation of a methodology to simulate interobserver variability.
abstract: Objective. Contouring for radiotherapy planning remains time intensive. As such, interobserver contour variation (IOV) studies are limited in patient and/or observer numbers ([Guzene et al (2023 Int. J. Radiat. Oncol. 115 1047-60)]). This study provides a methodology to simulate IOV on images containing a single contour. Approach. 14 gynaecological cancer radiotherapy target volumes delineated by five observers on T2W-MRI scans were used to develop an AI-based approach and three rule-based (simple, normal, adapted) approaches to generate estimated minimum and maximum (min/max) contours. The rule-based approaches used delineation uncertainty of the observers' contours. The AI-based approach combined seven nnU-Net models into an ensemble. The development of the AI-based and rule-based approaches utilised 7-fold and leave-one-out cross validation, respectively. Validation used a separate/second dataset with the same characteristics and six observers. A single contour was used as the basis and the remaining five contours were used to generate the min/max contours. Performance of each approach was assessed using dice similarity coefficient (DSC), mean surface distance (MSD), surface DSC (sDSC) and Hausdorff distance. The best approach was utilised in a pipeline to generate a min/max contour. Multiple contours were generated between these by applying non-uniform expansions and contractions to a single contour. The comparison metrics of the observers' and simulated contours were computed in pairwise, with a mean and standard deviation calculated. Main results . The adapted rule-based approach performed best across all metrics and was used in the subsequent pipeline. The AI-based approach had comparative median values to the rule-based approaches, but a much wider range of values. The observers' and simulated contours had a DSC of 0.77 ± 0.13 and 0.78 ± 0.20, respectively and an MSD of 2.4 ± 1.7 mm and 2.2 ± 1.5 mm, respectively. Significance. This study provides a methodology to generate additional observer contours from a single observer contour based on IOV data.

title: Arbitrary-Scale Super-Resolution for Non-Contrast Coronary MRA via Wavelet-Laplacian Enhanced Implicit Network.
abstract: Non-contrast coronary magnetic resonance angiography (NC-CMRA) provides a radiation-free and contrast-free approach for coronary assessment, but its diagnostic value is limited by insufficient spatial resolution. We propose an arbitrary-scale super-resolution framework that integrates a physiology-aware degradation model with a Wavelet-Laplacian Enhanced Implicit Network (WLEI-Net). The degradation model sequentially represents heart-rate-variability-driven asymmetric cardiac motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck respiratory translation, cardiopulmonary coupling, band-limited k-space noise, and Rician magnitude formation, and is designed to better represent the coupled physiological and k-space effects of clinical acquisitions. WLEI-Net combines SwinIR feature extraction, directional wavelet subband enhancement with channel attention, noise-adaptive Laplacian edge compensation, and a hybrid Charbonnier-wavelet-Sobel loss. Using 380 NC-CMRA images from 12 patients with a fixed patient-level split, the arbitrary-scale models were trained at 4.0× and evaluated at 2.0×, 2.5×, 3.0×, 3.5×, and 4.0×, with the four other evaluated scales unseen during training. WLEI-Net achieved the best mean performance for all six metrics at all five scales, and all comparisons against the four baselines remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction (BH-adjusted p ≤ 0.012). In a blinded two-reader evaluation of 57 test images at 2.5× and 4.0×, WLEI-Net achieved the highest mean score for artifact/noise suppression, vascular edge integrity, and small-branch visibility, with ICC(2,2)=0.817-0.901. These results support internal reconstruction and reader-perceived image-quality benefits.

title: Structural MRI Morphometry Across the Alzheimer's Disease Spectrum: Classification and Generalization.
abstract: Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides quantitative measures of brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD), but reliable classification also depends on the evaluation protocol and performance across cohorts. This study assessed a morphometry-based approach for distinguishing cognitively normal (CN) participants, those with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and those with AD. The primary cohort included 815 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), with one screening MRI per participant and predefined training, validation, and test sets. MRI records were linked to FreeSurfer measurements using exact participant and image identifiers. A multinomial L2-regularized logistic regression classifier used 42 predefined structural features and five-fold cross-validation grouped by acquisition site. In the held-out three-class test (n = 121), balanced accuracy was 0.6119 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.5291-0.6873) and the macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) was 0.7525. Recall was 0.8529 for CN, 0.2931 for MCI, and 0.6897 for AD. Additional development analyses examined demographic and clinical variables separately from the primary MRI-only result. For the binary transfer experiment, a separate ADNI-trained CN-versus-AD model using 32 shared morphometric features achieved balanced accuracy of 0.8458 and ROC-AUC of 0.9016 in site-grouped out-of-fold evaluation. The fixed model was then tested without target-cohort tuning on 181 older participants from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-1), grouped by Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR = 0 versus CDR > 0). External balanced accuracy was 0.6492 (95% CI: 0.5799-0.7158) and ROC-AUC was 0.7502. Because ADNI diagnoses and OASIS-1 CDR groups are not identical clinical endpoints, the external experiment was interpreted separately from the primary three-class analysis. The results demonstrate the value of reporting class-specific performance and independent-cohort evaluation when assessing structural MRI morphometry.

title: A conditional diffusion synthesis of DWI and ADC maps for early stroke support.
abstract: Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of disability and mortality worldwide. Effective treatment is associated with fast and effective lesion quantification from image observations. NCCT is the common first imaging to discard other neurological conditions, but it has limited sensitivity for detecting early ischemic changes. In addition, DW-MRI studies are considered the gold standard for early lesion characterization through DWI sequences and ADC maps. Nonetheless, the analysis from MRI images is delayed, restricted for some patient conditions, and typically limited because of accessibility constraints. Although recent approaches have addressed these limitations by synthesizing DW-MRI from NCCT, they often fail to reproduce ischemic lesions. Moreover, their performance is usually reported with whole-image metrics, which can overestimate image quality. This work explores the capability of conditional diffusion models to synthesize DWI sequences and ADC maps from NCCT to support care protocols in early stroke scenarios. In particular, we explore both a direct synthesis from NCCT to ADC and a conditional cascade configuration. In the cascade, the NCCT is used as a conditioning input to generate synthetic DWI findings. Then, the corresponding ADC maps are generated from the synthetic DWI. The conditional diffusion models outperformed the U-Net, Pix2Pix and CycleGAN baselines in the brain region, reaching an SSIM of 0.53 for DWI and up to 0.36 for ADC. Direct diffusion achieved a higher global ADC fidelity than cascade diffusion (SSIM 0.87 vs. 0.83), whereas cascade diffusion obtained a lower ADC error within the lesion (MAE 0.19 vs. 0.22).

title: A Supervoxel Graph-Transformer Framework for Lightweight and Interpretable Brain Tumor Segmentation from Multimodal Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of brain tumor sub-regions from multimodal MRI is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning, but most deep learning methods process millions of voxels, which is computationally demanding. We propose TransformerGNN, a supervoxel graph-Transformer framework that reformulates volumetric segmentation as node classification on a sparse graph. Each multimodal volume (FLAIR, T1, T1ce, T2) is partitioned into approximately 2,000 SLIC supervoxels, reducing about 8.9 million voxels to a region adjacency graph whose nodes carry multimodal intensity and spatial features. Stacked TransformerConv layers combine graph connectivity with multi-head attention. On BraTS 2020, the model reaches a mean Dice of 0.9002 (WT 0.9579, TC 0.8393, ET 0.9033), and 0.893 } 0.005 across repeated runs. Paired ablation tests confirm the contribution of graph connectivity and, for whole-tumor and enhancing-tumor Dice, of attention. The model has 1.36 M parameters; its network forward pass takes 0.10 s on a 16 GB laptop and uses about 1.5 GB of memory, although end-to-end processing (about 32 s per volume) is dominated by supervoxel generation. Post-hoc gradient-based saliency provides regional, modality-level attributions whose clinical value remains to be validated.

title: Geometric Motion of Multiple Liver Targets in Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy: Analysis of Translational and Rotational Motion with Different Motion-Management and Isocenter techniques.
abstract: Background Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for multiple liver targets is challenged by respiratory motion and target positioning. This study compares interfraction and intrafraction translational and rotational motion across motion management strategies (MMS) and isocentre techniques in routine clinical practice. Materials and methods: A retrospective analysis included 103 patients with 2-11 liver targets treated with abdominal compression (AC), deep inspiration breath-hold (DIBH), or free breathing (FB). Pre- and mid-treatment Cone Beam CT (CBCT) images were registered to planning CT using liver-contour matching. Translational (Anteroposterior-AP, Craniocaudal-CC, Mediolateral-ML) and rotational (pitch, roll, yaw) shifts were analysed. Motion characteristics were compared across MMS and between single-isocenter (SIC) and multiple-isocenter (MIC) approaches. Results: A total of 1102 CBCT datasets (AC: 450; DIBH: 326; FB: 326) were analysed. Shifts in CC were consistently the largest translational component across MMS. AP motion was comparable between AC and DIBH but significantly lower in FB. DIBH showed higher pitch and roll deviations. MIC exhibited higher motion than SIC, with significance in AP (AC, FB) and yaw (FB), while DIBH showed no significant differences. Intrafraction and interfraction analyses indicated greater dispersion in CC and increased variability in DIBH and FB compared to AC. A strong positive correlation between roll and inter-target distance was observed in FB, with no significant associations in AC or DIBH. Conclusion: In multi-target liver SBRT, residual translational (≤5 mm) and rotational (≤2°) deviations persist despite CBCT verification. MMS and isocenter strategy influence motion, underscoring the need for careful technique selection and individualized margins.&#xD.

title: Can CT radiomics inform radiosensitizer prioritization? A low energy electron attachment screening study.
abstract: This study examines what pretreatment computed tomography (CT) radiomics would need to contribute to low energy electron (LEE) dissociative electron attachment (DEA) based radiosensitizer prioritization, using an auditable computational screening framework. From 421 patients with non-small-cell lung cancer in a public imaging collection, quality controlled masks yielded 107 PyRadiomics descriptors, which were reduced to 27. Standardized k-means gave a two group partition of 120 and 301 patients (mean silhouette 0.229) that exceeded a feature permutation null (p=0.0058) and showed fixed feature bootstrap Jaccard similarities of 0.88 and 0.93 (0.64 and 0.76 when feature selection was also resampled). The partition was organized along tumor volume, clinical tumor (T) category, scanner model and reconstruction kernel (unadjusted p<10 -4 for each); its nominal survival association was accounted for by stage and tumor volume (p=0.12), and ComBat harmonization for scanner model or reconstruction kernel gave size dominated or weakly separated alternatives. Five DEA records were combined with a constraint based 0-25 eV reference LEE distribution and a first order CT density factor. The ranking (5-bromouracil, 5-iodouridine, 5-fluorouridine, 2-nitrofuran, catechin sulfate) follows the input cross sections: the CT density factor rescales all scores by a common factor, and the order stayed the same under every density and resonance width variation and every random LEE spectrum tested. Monte Carlo propagation identified 5-bromouracil and 5-iodouridine as a stable leading pair (rank 1 in 69% and 31%) and catechin sulfate as consistently last, while the order of 5-fluorouridine and 2-nitrofuran depended on reported temperature effects. Changing the ranking would require the 0-1 eV share of the electron spectrum to fall below 1% (reference value 27%). CT radiomics could therefore inform prioritization once phenotype specific electron spectra, energy resolved cross sections and biological validation are available.

The partition was organized along tumor volume, clinical tumor (T) category, scanner model and reconstruction kernel (unadjusted p<10<sup>-4</sup>for each); its nominal survival association was accounted for by stage and tumor volume (p=0.12), and ComBat harmonization for scanner model or reconstruction kernel gave size dominated or weakly separated alternatives. Five DEA records were combined with a constraint based 0-25 eV reference LEE distribution and a first order CT density factor. The ranking (5-bromouracil, 5-iodouridine, 5-fluorouridine, 2-nitrofuran, catechin sulfate) follows the input cross sections: the CT density factor rescales all scores by a common factor, and the order stayed the same under every density and resonance width variation and every random LEE spectrum tested. Monte Carlo propagation identified 5-bromouracil and 5-iodouridine as a stable leading pair (rank 1 in 69% and 31%) and catechin sulfate as consistently last, while the order of 5-fluorouridine and 2-nitrofuran depended on reported temperature effects. Changing the ranking would require the 0-1 eV share of the electron spectrum to fall below 1% (reference value 27%). CT radiomics could therefore inform prioritization once phenotype specific electron spectra, energy resolved cross sections and biological validation are available.

title: An interpretable physics-informed graph neural network for forecasting longitudinal tau progression in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Forecasting the progression of tau pathology by modeling its spatiotemporal dynamics is critical for characterizing Alzheimer's disease (AD), where tau is a key driver of disease progression. Tau is an important prognostic biomarker for AD and is a primary endpoint for many ongoing clinical therapeutic trials. Tau burden can be quantified in vivo using positron emission tomography (PET), while its propagation is hypothesized to follow the structural connectome derived from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), providing a framework for modeling network-driven tau spread. Deep learning approaches, particularly graph neural networks (GNNs), enable data-driven learning of regional changes in tau burden by leveraging brain connectivity. However, purely data-driven models are prone to overfitting and may fail to capture biologically meaningful propagation patterns. To address this, we present here a physics-informed GNN framework for tau forecasting that incorporates prior models of tau propagation, specifically the Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov (FKPP) equation and the epidemic spreading model (ESM), as regularization terms in the latent space of the network. Our analysis relies on PET and DTI data from N=462 amyloid-positive human subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Our results demonstrate that physics-informed models improve model performance over the unregularized baseline across multiple evaluation metrics, with regularization in the latent space improving robustness compared to that in the feature space. The FKPP formulation achieves the best mean predictive performance, followed closely by ESM. We further implement post-hoc interpretability using Integrated Gradients to identify key regions and connections driving the model's predictions. The interpretability analysis is consistent with the observed performance gains, indicating that physics-based regularization yields more localized attribution within biologically relevant regions. Overall, our findings demonstrate that integrating prior formulations of tau propagation with GNNs enhances predictive accuracy and interpretability, providing a promising framework for modeling network-driven spread of tau pathology.

title: Optimizing Rib Remodeling: A Data-Driven Model for Personalized Waist Contouring.
abstract: Background Rib cage remodeling procedures, like rib osteotomy with osteosynthesis, have shown promise for waist narrowing in aesthetic surgery. However, the ideal osteotomy location and bending angle remain poorly defined. Objectives This preclinical, proof-of-concept study aimed to: (1) quantify how osteotomy location and rib bending angle affect rib apex displacement using a large, computed tomography (CT) dataset, and (2) develop a data-driven framework as a first step toward guiding selection of rib number, osteotomy site, and bending angle tailored to individual waist contour goals. Methods Using the open-source RibFrac CT dataset, 600 ribs (300 eleventh [XI] and 300 tenth [X]) were segmented with the RibSeg deep learning tool. A custom MATLAB script simulated 15 bending scenarios per rib by varying osteotomy location (7 cm, 8 cm, 9 cm from midline) and bending angles (10°, 20°, 30°, 45°, 55°). Displacement at the rib apex was computed using a chord-perpendicular method. A graphical user interface (GUI) allowed for manual interaction, and a linear mixed-effects model quantified the effects of angle, osteotomy location, and their interaction. Results Both bending angle and osteotomy distance significantly affected apex displacement (p < 0.001), with a negative interaction indicating reduced effect of angle at more lateral osteotomy points. Rib X showed greater displacement overall than rib XI. Conclusions This proof-of-concept model establishes a biomechanical foundation for individualized rib remodeling planning. While prospective clinical validation is needed, the framework is adaptable to patient-specific imaging across age, sex, and BMI, and may ultimately support personalized surgical decision-making.

title: A multi-reader multi-case study comparing Breast Cancer Reading Efficiency and Accuracy in Screening with Tomosynthesis versus AI-assisted mammography.
abstract: Objectives Full-field digital mammography (FFDM) is the standard for breast cancer screening but has reduced sensitivity in dense breasts. Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) improves cancer detection compared to 2D mammography but is limited by cost and longer reading times. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced mammography has demonstrated improved sensitivity compared to 2D mammography. This study compares AI-enhanced 2D mammography (DM+AI) with DBT in recalling interval breast cancers (IBCs). Methods : A multi-reader, multi-case crossover study was conducted using the Emory BrEast Imaging Dataset, which includes paired FFDM and DBT images with biopsy-proven outcomes. Six radiologists reviewed 53 IBC and 53 screen-detected cancer (SDC) cases, with random assignment to DM+AI or DBT, followed by crossover after a washout period. Primary outcomes included recall rate of IBCs. Secondary outcomes included recall rate of SDCs, interpretation time, and subgroup analysis by breast density. Results : For IBCs, DM+AI and DBT demonstrated similar recall rates (41.5% vs 40.9%) and detection rates (14.8% vs 11.9%). DM+AI identified more non-invasive (31.5% vs 13.0%) and mass-forming (61.0% vs 21.8%) cancers. For SDCs, recall and detection rates were comparable across modalities. In fatty breasts, recall was higher with DM+AI (91.7% vs 50.0%), while DBT performed better in extremely dense breasts. DM+AI enabled faster interpretation, averaging 24.1 seconds less per case. Conclusion : AI-enhanced 2D mammography demonstrated comparable performance to DBT with shorter interpretation times, supporting a stratified screening approach. Advances in knowledge This study is the first direct comparison of AI-enhanced mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis for IBC detection.

title: Quantitative Hepatobiliary MRI for Early Prognostic Assessment After Liver Transplantation: Survival Prediction Using the Contrast Enhancement Index.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the feasibility and prognostic value of the contrast enhancement index (CEI) derived from gadobenate dimeglumine (Gd-BOPTA)-enhanced hepatobiliary-phase (HBP) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for early assessment of liver graft function after liver transplantation (LT). Methods This retrospective study included LT recipients undergoing Gd-BOPTA-enhanced MRI within 6 months after transplantation. CEI was calculated using liver-to-psoas signal intensity ratios on pre-contrast and HBP images acquired 90-120 minutes after contrast administration. ROC, Kaplan-Meier, and age-adjusted Cox regression analyses evaluated associations with mortality. Results Seventy patients (median age, 62 years; interquartile range [IQR], 48-74) were included. CEI was quantifiable in all cases (median, 1.27; IQR, 1.09-1.37). Non-survivors had significantly lower CEI values than survivors (median, 1.17 vs 1.31; p = 0.03; Cliff's δ = -0.28). ROC analysis showed moderate discrimination for mortality (AUC, 0.667; 95% CI, 0.529-0.793), with an optimal cutoff of 1.301 (sensitivity, 88%; specificity, 51.2%). Patients with CEI <1.301 had significantly lower overall survival (log-rank p = 0.028). After adjustment for recipient age, CEI remained associated with mortality (HR per 0.1-unit increase, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.98; p = 0.035). Conclusion Quantitative CEI measurement on Gd-BOPTA HBP MRI is feasible after LT, and lower CEI values. Advances in knowledge This study links quantitative Gd-BOPTA-enhanced HBP MRI with overall survival after LT, supporting CEI as a potential non-invasive imaging biomarker for postoperative risk stratification.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Procedural Efficiency of ACR TI-RADS, EU-TIRADS, and K-TIRADS in ≤ 10 mm Thyroid Nodules Using Bethesda Cytology: A Cohort of 998 Nodules.
abstract: Objectives To compare the diagnostic performance and procedural efficiency of American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (ACR TI-RADS), European Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (EU-TIRADS), and Korean Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (K-TIRADS) in ≤ 10 mm nodules using Bethesda cytology as the reference standard. Methods This retrospective study included 998 nodules ≤10 mm undergoing ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB). Primary analyses included Bethesda II (negative) and Bethesda V-VI (positive) nodules excluding Bethesda I/III/IV, yielding 604 nodules (540 negative; 64 positive). Categories 1-3 were considered low risk and 4-5 high risk under a harmonized threshold Diagnostic performance and classification patterns were compared. Results K-TIRADS showed the numerically highest sensitivity (93.8%) and negative predictive value (NPV) (97.9%), although sensitivity did not differ significantly between systems, with lower specificity (35.4%) and accuracy (41.6%).EU-TIRADS showed intermediate performans (sensitivity 68.8%, specificity 73.7%, accuracy 73.2%). ACR TI-RADS achieved the highest specificity (83.3%) and accuracy (81.0%) with lower sensitivity (60.9%). Low-risk classification rates were 78.6% (ACR), 69.2% (EU), and 32.3% (K) of nodules; false-positive high-risk classifications among Bethesda II nodules were 16.7%, 26.3%, and 64.6%, respectively. Conclusion In ≤ 10 mm nodules, the three systems demonstrated distinct diagnostic and classification profiles under a harmonized TR4-5 threshold, with different trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity. Advances in knowledge Applying a harmonized TR4-5 threshold in ≤ 10 mm nodules reveals substantially differences in classification patterns among the three systems, demonstrating that they are not interchangeable under a uniform risk threshold.

title: Construction and Validation of a Prediction Model for TACE Resistance in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Based on Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Radiomics.
abstract: Objective To construct and validate a contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) radiomics-clinical model for predicting transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods A total of 168 HCC patients who underwent CEUS on two vendor platforms (Philips E9 and GE Logiq E95) were split into a training set (n = 118) and an internal validation set (n = 50), with an additional 80 patients forming an external validation cohort. For each patient, 2D regions of interest were manually delineated on the largest cross-sectional slice of each CEUS phase. Radiomic features were extracted and screened by LASSO regression; the twelve retained features were linearly combined into a single Rad-score. The Rad-score and three prespecified clinical risk factors (tumor size, Child-Pugh class, AFP) confirmed by multivariate analysis were combined into a parsimonious logistic regression (LR) model with four predictors in total. Performance was assessed by ROC curve, calibration curve, decision curve analysis (DCA), subgroup analysis, and prospective validation. Results The combined model had AUCs of 0.895, 0.891 and 0.846 in three sets, with subgroup AUCs >0.86. Prospective validation showed TACE plus sorafenib improved 6-month response rate from 26.7% to 53.3% for high-risk patients. Conclusion The CEUS radiomics-clinical model accurately predicts TACE resistance, guiding individualized HCC treatment. Advances in knowledge This model integrates CEUS multi-phase radiomics and clinical factors, outperforming single clinical/radiomic models. Strict multi-step screening and comprehensive validation avoid data leakage, ensuring robust prediction and clinical translatability.

Results

The combined model had AUCs of 0.895, 0.891 and 0.846 in three sets, with subgroup AUCs >0.86. Prospective validation showed TACE plus sorafenib improved 6-month response rate from 26.7% to 53.3% for high-risk patients.

Conclusion

The CEUS radiomics-clinical model accurately predicts TACE resistance, guiding individualized HCC treatment.

Advances in knowledge

This model integrates CEUS multi-phase radiomics and clinical factors, outperforming single clinical/radiomic models. Strict multi-step screening and comprehensive validation avoid data leakage, ensuring robust prediction and clinical translatability.

title: Multiparametric MRI Tumor Habitat Analysis for Differentiating Non-Enhancing IDH-Wildtype Glioblastoma from Low-Grade Glioma.
abstract: Objectives To investigate whether voxel-wise multiparametric physiologic MRI-based tumor habitat analysis captures intratumoral heterogeneity that differentiates non-enhancing glioblastoma (GBM) from low-grade glioma (LGG) beyond clinical and conventional imaging features. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 84 patients with non-enhancing gliomas (42 GBM, 42 LGG) from November 2007 to October 2024. An external validation cohort from Institution 2 (n = 14; 8 GBM, 6 LGG) was also included. Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV), and volume transfer constant (Ktrans) maps were used to construct voxel-wise habitat clustering via k-means and to extract the 10th and 90th percentiles, mean, and median values. Statistical analyses comprised survival analyses, logistic regression, and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results Voxel-wise clustering delineated six distinct spatial habitats. GBMs were enriched in hypercellular, hypervascular, high-permeability habitats, whereas LGGs predominantly occupied hypocellular, hypovascular, low-permeability habitats. Stratification based on the proportion of high-risk habitat clusters revealed significantly shorter progression-free survival in patients with higher cluster burden (P <.05). The multiparametric model combining ADC, rCBV, and Ktrans achieved the highest AUC (0.83) for differentiating non-enhancing GBM from LGG, compared with 0.59-0.71 for demographic and VASARI-based comparator models. Conclusions Multiparametric MRI-based voxel-wise habitat analysis enables accurate, noninvasive differentiation of non-enhancing glioblastoma from low-grade glioma while demonstrating potential prognostic relevance based on intratumoral physiologic heterogeneity. Advances in knowledge This study presents a novel voxel-wise multiparametric MRI habitat analysis integrating diffusion, perfusion, and permeability to capture intratumoral heterogeneity in non-enhancing gliomas, thereby improving diagnostic differentiation and potential prognostic assessment beyond conventional imaging methods.

title: Volumetric fat fraction quantification of the sacroiliac joint: changes in axial spondyloarthritis.
abstract: Objectives To investigate the changes of fat fraction in the sacroiliac joint in axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), including both the cartilaginous joint and the posterior ligamentous joint (PSIJ), by using a volumetric analyzing method on proton-density fat fraction (PDFF) maps. Methods Patients aged 18-45 years with low back pain that underwent a 3.0 T MRI scan of the sacroiliac joint with additional PDFF maps were retrospectively included. Semi-automatic segmentation of the subcortical region and the PSIJ was performed. Volumetric fat fraction parameters were quantified including histographic analysis. Comparison between axSpA and non-SpA patients was performed. Results Ninety-three patients including 44 axSpA and 49 non-SpA patients were included. Patients with axSpA had higher mean sacrum PDFF (58.2% vs. 52.5%, p = 0.004). The percentage of bone volume with PDFF ranged from 75% to 100% (i.e. PDFF75100) increased (24.0% vs. 8.9%, p < 0.001), while the percentages of PDFF2550 and PDFF5075 decreased (26.6% vs. 35.6%, p = 0.005, 33.7% vs. 42.0%, p < 0.001). The mean ilium PDFF was not different between groups (p = 0.284), while the percentage of PDFF5075 decreased (39.0% vs. 46.3%, p = 0.033) and the percentage of PDFF75100 increased (20.6% vs.10.6%, p = 0.008). Fat fraction of the PSIJ was not changed in axSpA. The results remained unchanged after correction of age, sex and BMI. Conslusions By using a volumetric segmentation method, fat fraction of the cartilaginous sacroiliac joint was changed in axSpA while not the PSIJ. Advances in knowledge Changes of the fat fraction of both the cartilaginous and ligamentous sacroiliac joint was described in detail using a semi-automatic segmentation method.

title: Disruptions in brain hierarchical organization reveal Alzheimer's disease progression.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease arises from interacting amyloid, tau and neurodegenerative processes and is associated with large-scale network dysfunction and reduced brain dynamics complexity. However, it remains unclear whether disease progression alters the causal hierarchical organization of large-scale brain dynamics. We examined hierarchical brain organization across the Alzheimer's disease continuum using multimodal neuroimaging from 134 participants in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (46 amyloid-negative cognitively normal, 36 amyloid-positive cognitively normal, 31 amyloid-positive mild cognitive impairment and 21 amyloid-positive Alzheimer's disease dementia; mean age 73.9 ± 6.2 years). Participants underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging and positron emission tomography, with amyloid and tau imaging available in 121 individuals. We estimated the generative effective connectivity using whole-brain modelling and quantified hierarchy through trophic levels and directedness using an ecology-inspired framework. Group differences were assessed using non-parametric permutation testing with covariate adjustment and false discovery rate correction. A supervised machine learning framework using logistic regression with nested cross-validation and Monte Carlo resampling evaluated whether hierarchical features could classify disease stage. Associations with amyloid, tau burden and grey matter volume and cognitive performance were examined using mixed-effects ridge regression and multiple linear regression adjusted for age, gender, education and APOE -ɛ4 carrier status. Amyloid-negative cognitively normal exhibited a well-stratified hierarchy in which somatomotor and frontoparietal regions acted as sources, the default mode network occupied an intermediate integrative position, and memory, limbic and visual systems acted as sinks. Across the clinical spectrum, we observed a progressive flattening of hierarchical organization, characterized by reduced trophic levels in the somatomotor, salience, control and default mode networks, and increased hierarchical positioning of visual and thalamic regions. Hierarchical features classified disease stage, including the preclinical distinction between amyloid-negative and amyloid-positive cognitively normal, indicating sensitivity to early stages. Hierarchical alterations were associated with amyloid, tau and neurodegeneration. Moreover, they predicted cognitive impairment across all clinical tests. These findings suggest that Alzheimer's pathology selectively disrupts hierarchical brain organization. Our ecology-inspired framework offers a sensitive, non-invasive approach linking molecular pathology to large-scale network reconfiguration and cognitive decline, providing additional information beyond conventional correlation-based or graph-theoretical metrics, revealing its potential as a neuroimaging marker for early detection and disease staging across the Alzheimer's continuum.

title: Cervical and thoracic spinal cord grey and white matter atrophy: a longitudinal study in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons. Spinal cord (SC) MRI metrics have been suggested as potential biomarkers in ALS, but longitudinal data elucidating the development of cervical and thoracic SC grey matter (GM) and white matter (WM) atrophy remain limited. Radially sampled Averaged Magnetization Inversion Recovery Acquisitions (rAMIRA) enable the investigation of SC substructures. The objective was to investigate longitudinal changes in cervical and thoracic SC MRI metrics in patients with ALS compared with healthy age- and sex-matched controls (HC) using rAMIRA imaging and to examine the relationship of these changes with clinical phenotype and functional decline. Forty-one patients with ALS and 41 age- and sex-matched HC underwent rAMIRA MRI at baseline and every 6 months for up to 24 months. Axial SC images were acquired at intervertebral disc levels C2/C3-C5/C6 and the thoracic enlargement (T max ) level. SC total cross-sectional area (TCA), GM area (GMA) and WM areas (WMA) were segmented and analysed using linear mixed-effects models to compare longitudinal changes between groups. Associations between longitudinal changes in SC metrics, clinical phenotype and ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) were examined. At baseline, patients with ALS exhibited significant TCA, GMA and WMA reductions at cervical and thoracic levels compared with HC, except for WMA at T max . Over 24 months, significant longitudinal TCA and GMA decline was observed at multiple cervical and thoracic levels. WMA significantly declined only at level C3/C4. Stratification by disease onset revealed distinct patterns: patients with bulbar onset showed preserved cervical SC area metrics over 12 months, whereas those with cervical and lumbar onset exhibited marked TCA, GMA and WMA SC decline. Longitudinal TCA, GMA and WMA reductions correlated with 12-month ALSFRS-R decline. These findings suggest that SC imaging metrics reflect the functional impact of ALS. rAMIRA imaging allows detection of significant cervical and thoracic SC atrophy in ALS over 12 and 24 months. SC TCA and GMA atrophy is most pronounced in areas corresponding to symptom onset and is linked to overall clinical disability. SC imaging, capturing both GM and WM changes, represents a promising tool for monitoring disease progression and may inform the multimodal development of future imaging markers in ALS. Future studies with larger cohorts and earlier disease stages are warranted to validate these findings.

title: Brain network overlap as a predictor of depressive symptoms.
abstract: The brain's network architecture supports emotion and cognition and is disrupted in mental disorders, including major depressive disorder. Traditional network models often assign each brain region to a single dominant network. However, accumulating evidence supports an overlapping organization in which regions participate in several networks. Here, we tested whether network overlap (i) is altered in major depressive disorder, (ii) is modulated by a dopaminergic pharmacological challenge and (iii) predicts depressive symptoms. To this end, we evaluated 111 unmedicated individuals (ages: 18-48 years; 84.6% women), including 53 with current major depressive disorder and 58 healthy controls. Prior to functional MRI scanning, participants received either 50 mg of amisulpride, a low-dose dopamine D2/D3 antagonist that enhances dopaminergic signalling, or placebo in a double-blind, randomized design. Approximately 1 h later, coinciding with peak plasma concentration, participants completed a reward task in the scanner. Individualized cortical parcellations were derived from functional MRI data, followed by edge-centric connectomes. Specifically, functional connections (edges) were clustered into communities, allowing brain regions to participate in multiple networks. Entropy and functional diversity were computed to quantify network overlap within canonical large-scale brain systems. Three-way mixed ANOVA (diagnosis, drug, canonical brain system) tested the effects of major depressive disorder and dopamine on network overlap. Elastic net regression was applied to predict depression severity and anhedonia from network overlap measures. Individuals with major depressive disorder exhibited greater functional diversity, indicating reduced similarity in connectivity profiles among regions assigned to the same brain system. Across all participants, dopamine tended to reduce brain entropy, providing preliminary evidence for a less overlapping network organization. Measures of network overlap predicted anhedonia and depression severity, with limbic and visual networks contributing most strongly. Collectively, these findings indicate that individual differences in brain network overlap track depressive symptomatology and are sensitive to dopaminergic modulation. Ultimately, these measures may serve as markers for monitoring disease progression and predicting clinical outcomes.

Specifically, functional connections (edges) were clustered into communities, allowing brain regions to participate in multiple networks. Entropy and functional diversity were computed to quantify network overlap within canonical large-scale brain systems. Three-way mixed ANOVA (diagnosis, drug, canonical brain system) tested the effects of major depressive disorder and dopamine on network overlap. Elastic net regression was applied to predict depression severity and anhedonia from network overlap measures. Individuals with major depressive disorder exhibited greater functional diversity, indicating reduced similarity in connectivity profiles among regions assigned to the same brain system. Across all participants, dopamine tended to reduce brain entropy, providing preliminary evidence for a less overlapping network organization. Measures of network overlap predicted anhedonia and depression severity, with limbic and visual networks contributing most strongly. Collectively, these findings indicate that individual differences in brain network overlap track depressive symptomatology and are sensitive to dopaminergic modulation. Ultimately, these measures may serve as markers for monitoring disease progression and predicting clinical outcomes.

title: Seeing the Gaps: Heatmaps, Metrics, and the Hidden Failures of Explainable AI in Dentomaxillofacial Radiology - A Systematic Review.
abstract: Objectives This systematic review aims to evaluate the techniques and reported patterns of heatmap-based visual explanations in deep learning (DL) systems for dental radiographic classification tasks. Methods A literature search following PRISMA guidelines was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore Library, Oria.no and Google Scholar to retrieve studies using DL for dental classification tasks. Only articles with a visual explanation (heatmap) were selected. Risk of bias assessment was done with QUADAS-2, PROBAST-AI and CEBM. The heatmap technique, reasons for inclusion, explanations provided and patterns were analysed. Results In the 136 studies reviewed, Grad-CAM was the most commonly used technique. The predominant reason for using visual explanations was to understand the decision-making process of the DL model. Some heatmaps reflect established radiographic criteria, while others exhibit unique, label-dependent patterns that sometimes emphasise irrelevant areas. Cropping to the region of interest influences visual explanations. Conclusions Visual explanations seem clinically plausible to domain experts when aligned with domain knowledge, but clinical plausibility does not equal technical faithfulness. Formal faithfulness testing was rarely performed among the included studies. Therefore, explanations should not be assumed to accurately represent the model's underlying reasoning. Limitations include the evaluation of studies not primarily designed for visual explanation assessment. No funding was received for this review. Authors declare no competing interests. Advances in knowledge Visual explanations, while clinically plausible when aligned with domain knowledge, remain insufficiently validated and should not be assumed to faithfully represent model reasoning. An implausible explanation does not necessarily indicate model failure. Domain/task-specific evaluation metrics for explainable AI in dentomaxillofacial radiology are needed.

title: Enhancing Cone-Beam Computed Tomography Image Quality Using Deep Learning-based Super-Resolution.
abstract: Objectives To develop deep learning super-resolution (SR) models for enhancing cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). Methods Seventy CBCT volumes (75 µm voxel size) served as references. Paired low-resolution (LR) volumes (300 µm) were simulated using physics-based degradation. Four architectures were each trained with three loss configurations (L1; L1+edge; L1+edge+perceptual): Swin Transformer for Image Restoration (SwinIR), Hybrid Attention Transformer (HAT), Hybrid Multi-Axis Aggregation Network (HMA-Net), and Dense-Residual-Connected Transformer (DRCT). Performance was assessed with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index measure (SSIM), learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), and deep image structure and texture similarity (DISTS). Three dentists ranked the 12 configurations in 28 sets using blinded forced-choice pairwise comparisons. Correlations of metrics and expert ranks were assessed using Spearman correlation. Results All configurations outperformed LR input and bicubic interpolation on every metric (p < 0.05). HMA-Net trained with L1+edge+perceptual loss performed best on LPIPS (0.216) and DISTS (0.186). HAT with L1 loss achieved the highest PSNR (28.79 dB) and SSIM (0.820). Experts ranked DRCT and HAT with L1 loss, and DRCT with L1+edge loss, as the best configurations (p < 0.001 versus others). Expert rank correlated moderately only with PSNR (rho = -0.65) and SSIM (rho = -0.60; both p < 0.05). Conclusions Transformer-based SR improved the perceived quality of clinical CBCT images. HAT and DRCT trained with L1 pixel loss alone, and DRCT trained with L1 and edge loss, demonstrated superior performance. Advances in knowledge Transformer-based super-resolution improved expert-perceived detail of simulated low-resolution in vivo CBCT scans without additional radiation dose, supporting further validation on directly acquired low-resolution scans.

title: Lessons learned from a decade of EUS(-FNA) staging in esophageal and GEJ carcinoma: towards a selective staging strategy.
abstract: Endoscopic ultrasonography with fine-needle aspiration (EUS(-FNA)) is recommended by current guidelines as part of the staging for esophageal and gastro-esophageal junction (GEJ) carcinoma, yet its incremental value over modern 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) remains uncertain. This Lessons Learned article reflects on over a decade of EUS(-FNA) and FDG-PET staging in 402 patients with potentially curable esophageal or GEJ carcinoma at a high-volume tertiary referral center. In 91.3% of patients, EUS(-FNA) did not alter the radiation field as would have been defined by FDG-PET. EUS(-FNA) resulted in an expansion of the radiation field in 4.5% and reduction in 4.2% of patients. Squamous cell carcinoma showed more than two-fold greater likelihood of radiation field modification. Among 193 patients classified as FDG-PET non-suspicious for malignant lymph nodes (LNs), EUS-FNA identified malignant LNs in eight patients (4.1%), which influenced the radiation field. In 5 of 402 patients (1.2%) a malignant LN was detected with EUS-FNA in a station that would not have routinely been resected surgically. In patients planned for neoadjuvant or definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT), LN staging is of direct therapeutic consequence: underestimation of nodal disease may result in geographic miss, while overestimation leads to unnecessary irradiation. In contrast, in patients treated with perioperative 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin and docetaxel (FLOT) followed by surgical lymphadenectomy, most involved LN stations are routinely addressed surgically, limiting the added value of EUS(-FNA) for treatment planning. Therefore, we view EUS(-FNA) as a selective staging tool in patients planned for neoadjuvant or definitive CRT, rather than a procedure applied routinely to all patients.

title: Not all inflammation is equal: biomarker-structural discordance and flare risk in clinically stable small-bowel Crohn's disease.
abstract: Background Patients with clinically stable small-bowel Crohn's disease (SB-CD) may harbor heterogeneous residual inflammation. We performed the first study characterizing inflammatory burden with video capsule endoscopy (VCE), intestinal ultrasound (IUS), and biomarkers, comparing their prognostic performance. Methods Pooled analysis of 3 prospective cohorts of adults with SB-CD in remission/mild symptoms (Crohn's disease activity index [CDAI] < 220) undergoing concurrent VCE, IUS, C-reactive protein (CRP), and fecal calprotectin (FCP) assessment. Primary outcome: inflammation-driven CD flare ≥6 months from baseline. Unsupervised clustering identified inflammatory clusters (n = 87); outcome analyses included 81 patients with follow-up. Results Among 87 patients (median age 31, 57% male), 3 clusters emerged: low-burden (n = 48), biomarker-predominant (n = 18; markedly elevated FCP/CRP, preserved bowel wall thickness [BWT], intermediate Lewis score [LS]), and concordant-active (n = 21; uniform elevation across modalities). Twenty flare events (25%) occurred at median 12.5 months. Concordant-active carried higher flare risk than low-burden (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 2.67, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01-7.11), while biomarker-predominant showed no significant excess risk (HR 1.00). In the SB-restricted comparison, SB-BWT plus FCP showed discrimination comparable to LS (C-index 0.635 vs. 0.596), and LS did not add to this combination (likelihood ratio test P = .223). Whole-bowel BWT ≥ 4.3 mm added to LS (P = .008), whereas SB-BWT ≥3.8 mm did not (P = .384). Conclusions Isolated biomarker elevation without structural activity was not associated with significant excess flare risk in clinically stable SB-CD, while concordant activity showed higher risk requiring larger-cohort confirmation. Within the SB, IUS plus FCP showed no significant difference in prognostic performance compared with VCE, with whole-bowel IUS additionally contributing colonic transmural information not captured by the LS.

title: Liver radiomics on routine cardiac CT identifies hepatic stress states that predict heart failure.
abstract: Aims Heart failure (HF) prevention remains limited because early multisystem cardiometabolic dysfunction is not captured by conventional risk tools. We evaluated whether liver radiomic phenotypes derived opportunistically from coronary artery calcium computed tomography (CAC-CT) identify imaging-defined hepatic stress states associated with incident HF. Methods and results We analysed 59 237 individuals undergoing CAC-CT (CLARIFY: 46 028; Houston Methodist: 13 209). Liver regions were segmented and radiomic features extracted to derive a Liver Radiomics Score (LRS). The model was trained in a CLARIFY derivation cohort (Dtr, n = 9205), validated in a hold-out cohort (Dts, n = 36 823), and externally evaluated in Houston Methodist (Dext, n = 13 209). The mean follow-up was 1411 days (SD 760.1) in the pooled Dtr and Dts cohorts (1144 HF events) and 470 days (SD 596) in Dext (212 HF events). Continuous LRS was associated with incident HF [Dts: hazard ratio (HR) 1.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.52-1.74; P < 0.001; Dext: HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.07; P = 0.004] and remained significant after multivariable adjustment in Dts. Increasing LRS quartiles showed progressively adverse hepatic, haemodynamic, and cardiometabolic profiles and higher HF risk. Among 17 806 Dts participants with PREVENT data, adding LRS modestly improved discrimination across CAC- and PREVENT-based models (P < 0.001) and improved reclassification metrics (7-year net reclassification improvement up to 0.25; including integrated discrimination improvement up to 0.015). High LRS identified elevated risk in low-risk groups: among participants with CAC=0, high LRS conferred ∼2.5-fold higher 5-year HF incidence, and ∼2.9-fold in PREVENT-low individuals. Conclusion In this large multicentre cohort, liver radiomics from CAC-CT captured hepatic stress states linked to HF risk and modestly improved risk stratification beyond CAC and PREVENT scores.

title: Long-term Prognostic Value of Sequential Coronary CT Angiography and Quantitative PET in Suspected Chronic Coronary Syndromes: A Multicentre study.
abstract: Background and aims The long-term prognostic value of a guideline-recommended selective sequential anatomical-functional imaging strategy using coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) followed by quantitative [15O]H2O positron emission tomography (PET) remains uncertain. We evaluated its long-term prognostic value in patients with first symptoms suggestive of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). Methods In this multicentre European cohort, symptomatic patients first underwent CCTA and were selectively referred to quantitative [15O]H2O PET in case of suspected obstructive stenosis (≥50%). Patients were stratified according to CCTA findings and PET-derived ischaemia (normal CCTA; non-obstructive CAD on CCTA; obstructive CAD on CCTA without ischaemia; obstructive CAD on CCTA with ischaemia). The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), and hospitalization for unstable angina (UA). Adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) were calculated. Results Among 3,918 patients (61.0±9.8 years; 54.3% female) with a median follow-up of 5.1 [3.8-8.0] years, 278 (7.1%) experienced the primary endpoint. aHRs increased stepwise across CCTA-PET categories. title: Sternal retraction-induced internal mammary artery graft flow impairment: intraoperative assessment and mechanistic insights: a case report.
abstract: Background The internal mammary artery (IMA) is the primary conduit for coronary revascularization, making reliable intraoperative flow assessment indispensable. We describe a rare case in which left IMA (LIMA) graft flow was compromised not by conduit or anastomotic issues but by sternal manipulation. Case summary A 76-year-old man undergoing emergency coronary artery bypass surgery reproducibly demonstrated markedly reduced LIMA flow only during wide sternal retraction. Intraoperatively, pronounced unilateral sternal retraction was noted, and postoperative computed tomography confirmed first- and second-rib fractures. Discussion These findings suggest a dynamic, retraction-dependent inflow disturbance, possibly related to deformation of the thoracic outlet and proximal subclavian artery. This case underscores the need for careful sternal manipulation, which may help avoid unnecessary graft revision or conduit replacement.

title: Fulminant myocarditis across the aetiological spectrum in the era of mechanical circulatory support: a case series.
abstract: Background Fulminant myocarditis is a rare but life-threatening condition characterized by acute haemodynamic compromise, malignant arrhythmias, and rapid progression to cardiogenic shock. Although the clinical presentation is often uniform, the underlying aetiology is heterogeneous and carries important implications for diagnosis, therapeutic strategy, and prognosis. Case summary We report four patients presenting within months of each other with fulminant myocarditis of distinct aetiologies: eosinophilic myocarditis associated with amoxicillin-clavulanate in a 71-year-old male; a suspected lymphocytic myocarditis in a 25-year-old male with a posthumously identified pathogenic FLNC (Filamin C) variant; lymphocytic myocarditis with extensive replacement fibrosis in a 68-year-old male; and virus-negative lymphocytic myocarditis in a 61-year-old female. All four required mechanical circulatory support. Outcomes ranged from death in two patients to survival with durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD) support in one and complete functional recovery after transient support in another. Conclusion Endomyocardial biopsy was pivotal in establishing the underlying diagnosis and guiding management. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) showed supporting findings but was most valuable raising the possibility of alternative diagnosis such as arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. These cases illustrate that fulminant myocarditis represents a haemodynamic phenotype rather than a final diagnosis. Systematic histological, virological, and-where clinically indicated-genetic evaluation is essential, as aetiology informs management but does not reliably predict outcome in mechanical circulatory support (MCS)-dependent presentations.

title: Trajectory of Pleural effusion and clinical outcomes in acute Heart Failure (TOP-HF): a prospective observational study.
abstract: Aims Pleural effusion (PE) is a common finding in acute heart failure (AHF). However, its trajectory and its prognostic implications have been poorly characterized. We aimed to evaluate the in-hospital and early post-discharge trajectory of PE and its association with clinical outcomes and health-related quality of life. Methods and results This prospective single-centre study included 100 patients hospitalized with AHF and PE at admission. Pleural effusion severity was serially assessed by thoracic ultrasound at admission, discharge, and 30, 90, and 180 days after discharge. The primary endpoint was the 180-day composite of all-cause death or worsening heart failure (WHF). Associations with PE trajectory were assessed using multivariable Cox regression. Health-related quality of life was evaluated with the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire. Median age was 88 years (interquartile range 83-92), 70% were women, and 80% had preserved ejection fraction. Pleural effusion improved during hospitalization in 59%; complete resolution occurred in 20% at discharge and 71.8% at 180 days. After adjustment, PE trajectory was not significantly associated with the composite endpoint [hazard ratio (HR) 1.30, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.69-2.45; P = 0.417], death (HR 2.34, 95% CI 0.84-6.47; P = 0.103), or WHF (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.61-2.35; P = 0.598). Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire trajectories did not differ significantly by PE trajectory. Conclusion Pleural effusion frequently improved during hospitalization and continued to resolve after discharge. Pleural effusion trajectory was not significantly associated with 180-day outcomes in this cohort, whereas residual B-lines at discharge were associated with adverse outcomes.

title: Growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15): a potential prognostic biomarker for medullary thyroid cancer patients.
abstract: Objective Growth Differentiation Factor 15 (GDF15) is a stress-induced cytokine that has been proposed as a biomarker in various cancers, with levels increasing alongside disease progression. GDF15 exerts its effects through binding to the GDNF family receptor α-like (GFRAL), which in turn binds to a pair of RET receptor, whose activation is primarily responsible of medullary thyroid cancer (MTC). Design This is a retrospective study. Methods Serum GDF15 levels were measured by ELISA in 161 patients with sporadic MTC and 47 normal control subjects. Associations between serum GDF15 levels and gender, body mass index (BMI), calcitonin (Ct), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), disease status, disease progression, and overall survival were analyzed. GDF15 mRNA expression was assessed in 96 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) MTC samples using Nanostring technology. Results Serum GDF15 levels were significantly higher in MTC patients compared to control subjects. They were more elevated in male and older patients, but no association with BMI was found. After adjusting for age and gender, GDF15 levels correlated with serum Ct and CEA levels. Elevated GDF15 levels were associated with more advanced disease status, but not with disease progression according to RECIST 1.1. Higher GDF15 levels predicted poorer overall survival both in the entire cohort and in patients with metastatic disease. Higher serum GDF15 levels were found in RET-mutant cases. At the transcriptomic level, metastatic MTC samples showed increased GDF15 mRNA expression. Positive correlation was found between GDF15 intratumoral mRNA and serum protein levels. Conclusions GDF15 might serve as a potential prognostic biomarker in MTC, associated with disease severity and survival. Given its signaling through the RET pathway, GDF15 could represent a relevant therapeutic and biological target in RET-driven MTC.
